description: Summarizes the arithmetic average and spread of a numeric variable.
when_to_use: Describe the center and variability of approximately symmetric numeric data.
assumptions: Requires meaningful numeric measurements; the mean and standard deviation are sensitive to extreme values.
example: Report participants' mean age and its standard deviation.

description: Summarizes the middle observation and spread of the middle half of a numeric distribution.
when_to_use: Describe skewed numeric data or variables with outliers.
assumptions: Requires observations that can be ordered; it does not assume normality.
example: Report median household income and its interquartile range.

description: Counts observations in categories and expresses their relative frequencies.
when_to_use: Describe the distribution of categorical variables.
assumptions: Requires consistently defined categories and an appropriate denominator.
example: Report the percentage of respondents who currently smoke.

description: Quantifies the strength and direction of a linear association between two numeric variables.
when_to_use: Explore linear associations between two continuous variables.
assumptions: Independent paired observations; approximately linear association; normality assumptions matter for small-sample inference.
example: Examine the correlation between height and weight.

description: Quantifies rank-based association between two variables.
when_to_use: Explore monotonic associations with ordinal or skewed numeric variables.
assumptions: Independent pairs; monotonicity for a meaningful single-direction interpretation.
example: Assess whether higher income rank accompanies higher health satisfaction.

description: Compares the means of two independent populations under a pooled-variance model.
when_to_use: Compare a numeric outcome between two unrelated groups with similar variability.
assumptions: Independent observations; approximately normal errors; equal group variances for the pooled test.
example: Compare mean systolic blood pressure between two separate groups.

description: Compares the means of two independent groups without assuming equal variances.
when_to_use: Compare two unrelated group means when variances or group sizes differ.
assumptions: Independent observations; approximate normality or adequate group sample sizes.
example: Compare mean earnings between two occupations with unequal variability.

description: Tests whether the mean within-pair difference is zero.
when_to_use: Compare two numeric measurements on the same people or matched pairs.
assumptions: Independent pairs; approximately normal distribution of within-pair differences.
example: Compare blood pressure before and after treatment in the same patients.

description: Compares how observations from two independent groups rank relative to one another.
when_to_use: Compare independent ordinal or continuous outcomes without assuming normality.
assumptions: Independent observations; similarly shaped distributions are needed for a simple median-shift interpretation.
example: Compare pain ratings between two unrelated treatment groups.

description: Tests whether a distribution of paired differences is centered around zero using signed ranks.
when_to_use: Compare paired ordinal or numeric measurements without relying on a paired t-test.
assumptions: Independent pairs; approximately symmetric distribution of nonzero paired differences.
example: Compare paired anxiety scores before and after therapy.

description: Tests whether mean numeric outcomes differ across levels of one categorical factor.
when_to_use: Compare a continuous outcome across three or more unrelated groups.
assumptions: Independent errors; approximately normal residuals; similar group variances.
example: Compare mean blood pressure across three dietary groups.

description: Tests main effects and interactions for two categorical factors on a continuous outcome.
when_to_use: Compare a continuous outcome across combinations of two categorical factors.
assumptions: Independent errors; approximately normal residuals; homogeneous within-cell variances.
example: Test diet, sex, and their interaction on weight change.

description: Tests mean differences across repeated conditions or times within the same subjects.
when_to_use: Compare repeated continuous measurements across three or more conditions.
assumptions: Independent subjects; approximately normal residuals; sphericity for standard univariate within-subject tests.
example: Compare cognition measured at four visits in the same participants.

description: Tests between-group, within-subject, and group-by-time effects in one model.
when_to_use: Compare trajectories across independent groups with repeated measurements.
assumptions: Independent subjects; approximately normal residuals; sphericity for relevant within-subject contrasts.
example: Compare treatment and control cognitive scores over four visits.

description: Compares outcome means across groups after adjustment for continuous covariates.
when_to_use: Compare group outcomes while adjusting for baseline or other measured covariates.
assumptions: Independent errors; linear covariate effects; suitable adjustment; common covariate slopes unless modeled otherwise.
example: Compare post-treatment scores adjusted for baseline scores.

description: Tests whether independent groups have the same rank distributions.
when_to_use: Compare ordinal or non-normal outcomes across three or more independent groups.
assumptions: Independent observations; similar distribution shapes for location or median interpretation.
example: Compare patient satisfaction ratings across four clinics.

description: Tests differences among repeated conditions using within-block ranks.
when_to_use: Compare three or more repeated ordinal or non-normal measures.
assumptions: Independent subjects or blocks; comparable matched measurements across conditions.
example: Compare repeated pain ratings at four scheduled visits.

description: Tests whether two categorical variables are statistically associated.
when_to_use: Analyze relationships between categorical variables in contingency tables.
assumptions: Independent observations; expected cell counts adequate for chi-square approximation.
example: Test association between smoking status and disease status.

description: Evaluates association in a contingency table using an exact conditional calculation.
when_to_use: Test categorical association in small or sparse tables.
assumptions: Independent observations; valid categorical classifications and conditional sampling setup.
example: Compare adverse-event occurrence across two small treatment groups.

description: Estimates the association of one predictor with the conditional mean of a numeric outcome.
when_to_use: Explain or predict a continuous outcome from one predictor.
assumptions: Correct mean function; independent errors or modeled dependence; appropriate variance assumptions for inference.
example: Predict systolic blood pressure from age.

description: Estimates adjusted associations between several predictors and a numeric outcome.
when_to_use: Explain or predict a continuous outcome from several variables.
assumptions: Suitable mean specification; independent or modeled errors; low problematic collinearity; appropriate inference assumptions.
example: Model blood pressure using age, body mass index, and smoking.

description: Models the probability of a binary outcome through a logit link.
when_to_use: Explain or predict outcomes with two possible values.
assumptions: Independent or appropriately clustered observations; correct logit specification; no complete separation.
example: Predict diabetes diagnosis from age, BMI, and activity.

description: Models expected event counts or rates using a log link.
when_to_use: Analyze nonnegative counts or event rates with exposure offsets.
assumptions: Appropriate conditional count process; mean-variance relationship near Poisson; independence or modeled dependence.
example: Model emergency admissions per person-year of follow-up.

description: Models continuous outcomes using fixed effects and subject- or cluster-level random effects.
when_to_use: Analyze repeated or hierarchical continuous measurements.
assumptions: Appropriate fixed and random effect structure; conditional residual assumptions; adequately supported clustering.
example: Model repeated cognitive scores nested within participants.

description: Models non-Gaussian outcomes with fixed effects and random effects.
when_to_use: Analyze clustered or repeated binary, count, or other generalized outcomes.
assumptions: Suitable link and response family; correctly specified grouping and random effects.
example: Model repeated infection outcomes among patients within clinics.

description: Finds orthogonal combinations of variables that capture the greatest observed variance.
when_to_use: Reduce the dimensionality of correlated numeric variables.
assumptions: Meaningful covariance structure; attention to variable scaling and outliers.
example: Reduce 30 correlated environmental indicators to a few components.

description: Estimates latent factors that account for shared covariance among measured variables.
when_to_use: Explore possible underlying constructs in a set of questionnaire items.
assumptions: Appropriate common-factor structure; sufficient shared correlations; estimator-specific assumptions.
example: Explore latent domains in a new wellbeing questionnaire.

description: Builds prediction rules by recursively splitting data into increasingly homogeneous groups.
when_to_use: Create interpretable classification or regression predictions.
assumptions: Representative training data; sufficient sample sizes; pruning or tuning to limit overfitting.
example: Classify diabetes risk from routine clinical measurements.

description: Combines predictions from many randomized decision trees.
when_to_use: Predict categorical or numeric outcomes with complex nonlinear relationships.
assumptions: Representative data; leakage-free validation; suitable handling of missing values.
example: Predict cardiovascular events using multiple clinical risk factors.

description: Estimates an intervention effect from the change in treated outcomes relative to comparison outcomes.
when_to_use: Evaluate policy or intervention effects when comparable untreated trends are plausible.
assumptions: Parallel untreated trends; no anticipation; no unaccounted time-varying confounding or composition changes.
example: Estimate the effect of a new local policy on hospital attendance.

description: Displays joint counts or proportions for combinations of categorical variables.
when_to_use: Describe how categories are distributed across groups.
assumptions: Well-defined categories and denominators; independent observations only if inferential tests follow.
example: Tabulate smoking status by age category.

description: Gives a range of parameter values compatible with a specified estimation procedure and confidence level.
when_to_use: Show uncertainty around means, proportions, differences, or model coefficients.
assumptions: Valid estimation method, sampling design, and interval procedure.
example: Report a 95% confidence interval for mean systolic blood pressure.

description: Measures rank concordance between two variables.
when_to_use: Assess ordinal association, particularly with small samples or ties.
assumptions: Independent paired observations; consistent handling of ties.
example: Compare agreement between two rankings of patient priorities.

description: Measures the linear association between a binary variable and a numeric variable.
when_to_use: Assess a numeric measure's association with a two-category indicator.
assumptions: Independent observations; meaningful binary coding; standard Pearson inferential conditions.
example: Associate examination score with pass/fail status.

description: Quantifies association between two variables after adjusting each for specified covariates.
when_to_use: Assess association while controlling for measured variables.
assumptions: Appropriate covariate specification; linear adjustment for Pearson partial correlation.
example: Correlate education and income after accounting for age.

description: Tests whether a sample mean differs from a prespecified value.
when_to_use: Compare a numeric outcome to an established reference mean.
assumptions: Independent observations; approximately normal observations or adequate sample size.
example: Test whether mean participant IQ differs from 100.

description: Tests differences among several group means without imposing equal variances.
when_to_use: Compare numeric outcomes across three or more independent groups with unequal variances.
assumptions: Independent observations; approximate within-group normality or suitable sample sizes.
example: Compare mean earnings across professions with unequal variance.

description: Tests group differences jointly across several correlated continuous outcomes.
when_to_use: Compare groups on multiple outcomes considered together.
assumptions: Independent cases; appropriate multivariate residual distribution and covariance structure.
example: Assess treatment differences in memory, attention, and processing speed.

description: Tests whether two paired binary measurements have equal marginal proportions.
when_to_use: Compare a yes/no outcome at two matched times or conditions.
assumptions: Independent pairs; exact version preferred when discordant pairs are few.
example: Assess change in smoking status before and after intervention.

description: Models curved predictor-outcome relationships using powers of predictors.
when_to_use: Model a nonlinear trend when a polynomial relationship is plausible.
assumptions: Appropriate polynomial degree; standard model error assumptions; avoid unsupported extrapolation.
example: Model changes in reaction time across age.

description: Models predictor effects using estimated smooth functions.
when_to_use: Estimate flexible nonlinear associations with outcomes of suitable distributions.
assumptions: Appropriate response family; smoothing choices; independent or modeled temporal/cluster dependence.
example: Estimate a nonlinear association between temperature and mortality.

description: Models probabilities of three or more unordered outcome categories.
when_to_use: Predict outcomes with multiple nominal categories.
assumptions: Independent or appropriately clustered observations; correct logit specification; identifiable coefficients.
example: Predict whether a commuter chooses car, bus, or train.

description: Models the probabilities of ordered response categories using cumulative logits.
when_to_use: Explain or predict ordered categorical outcomes.
assumptions: Proportional odds for the standard model; appropriate ordering and link.
example: Predict low, medium, or high treatment satisfaction.

description: Models overdispersed event counts with variance greater than the mean.
when_to_use: Analyze count outcomes with more variability than a Poisson model allows.
assumptions: Appropriate negative-binomial mean-variance form; independent or modeled dependence.
example: Model repeated emergency-department visit counts.

description: Combines a count model with a separate process generating additional zeros.
when_to_use: Analyze counts when a defensible second zero-generating process exists.
assumptions: Correct count distribution and zero-process specification; identifiable parameters.
example: Model absenteeism counts when some workers are never at risk of absence.

description: Models continuous proportion outcomes restricted to the open interval from zero to one.
when_to_use: Analyze fractional outcomes without exact zero or one values.
assumptions: Values strictly between zero and one; appropriate conditional beta distribution and link.
example: Model proportion of waking time spent sedentary.

description: Estimates effects on selected conditional quantiles rather than the mean.
when_to_use: Examine whether associations differ across low and high outcome levels.
assumptions: Correct conditional quantile specification; suitable uncertainty estimation.
example: Estimate education effects at the 10th and 90th income percentiles.

description: Estimates population-average regression effects while accounting for within-cluster correlation.
when_to_use: Analyze repeated or clustered outcomes when marginal effects are the focus.
assumptions: Correct mean model; independent clusters; adequate clusters for robust standard errors.
example: Estimate average treatment effects across repeated clinic visits.

description: Models relative event hazards as functions of predictors over follow-up time.
when_to_use: Estimate associations with time until an event under censoring.
assumptions: Proportional hazards; suitable censoring assumptions; independence or handled clustering.
example: Model time from enrollment to first cardiovascular event.

description: Estimates the probability of remaining event-free over time.
when_to_use: Describe survival or time-to-event distributions with censoring.
assumptions: Non-informative censoring; independent observations or valid handling of dependence.
example: Estimate survival after a cancer diagnosis.

description: Compares event-time distributions between groups using observed and expected events.
when_to_use: Compare survival curves for independent groups.
assumptions: Independent groups; non-informative censoring; greatest power often under proportional hazards.
example: Compare time to recurrence between treatment arms.

description: Tests whether observed variables fit a predefined latent factor structure.
when_to_use: Validate a hypothesized measurement model for a questionnaire.
assumptions: Identified measurement model; adequate data; appropriate estimator and distributional assumptions.
example: Evaluate whether a wellbeing scale fits three hypothesized factors.

description: Estimates a system of hypothesized directional relations among observed variables.
when_to_use: Test direct and indirect associations among measured variables.
assumptions: Identified and correctly specified path structure; estimator-appropriate assumptions.
example: Model education's association with health through employment and income.

description: Jointly estimates latent-variable measurement models and structural relationships.
when_to_use: Test relationships among multiple measured and latent constructs.
assumptions: Identifiable model; defensible specification; suitable estimator and sample size.
example: Model latent socioeconomic position, stress, and wellbeing.

description: Estimates indirect and direct paths between an exposure and outcome through a mediator.
when_to_use: Investigate hypothesized mechanisms connecting an exposure to an outcome.
assumptions: Correct temporal ordering; measured confounding control and stronger assumptions for causal mediation.
example: Estimate how exercise relates to mood through sleep quality.

description: Estimates average change trajectories and between-person differences in change.
when_to_use: Analyze repeated measurements to study growth or decline trajectories.
assumptions: Identified time structure; appropriate growth form; estimator-specific assumptions.
example: Estimate trajectories of cognitive function over five survey waves.

description: Models autocorrelation and differencing to describe or forecast a regularly spaced series.
when_to_use: Forecast or analyze univariate temporal data with serial dependence.
assumptions: Stationarity after appropriate differencing; residual autocorrelation adequately modeled.
example: Forecast monthly emergency department attendance.

description: Forecasts a time series using estimated level, trend, and seasonal components.
when_to_use: Forecast data with relatively stable trend or seasonal patterns.
assumptions: Suitable state-space error, trend, and seasonality structure.
example: Forecast the next six months of outpatient appointments.

description: Estimates changes in outcome level or trend following an intervention date.
when_to_use: Evaluate a policy introduced during a long sequence of repeated observations.
assumptions: Adequate pre/post measurement; correctly modeled trends and autocorrelation; no unaddressed concurrent events.
example: Estimate change in pollution following a traffic restriction.

description: Uses estimated treatment probabilities to balance observed characteristics between groups.
when_to_use: Adjust measured confounding in observational treatment comparisons.
assumptions: No unmeasured confounding for causal claims; overlap/positivity; appropriate balancing design.
example: Compare treated and untreated patients with similar baseline profiles.

description: Builds an ensemble of models sequentially to reduce predictive loss.
when_to_use: Predict complex outcomes from structured data with high accuracy.
assumptions: Representative data; leakage-free tuning; regularization to avoid overfitting.
example: Predict risk of hospital readmission from clinical records.

description: Shrinks regression coefficients toward zero using an L2 penalty.
when_to_use: Predict outcomes with many correlated predictors.
assumptions: Correct outcome model family; appropriate scaling and penalty tuning.
example: Predict income from strongly correlated socioeconomic indicators.

description: Uses an L1 penalty to shrink coefficients and select a subset of predictors.
when_to_use: Build parsimonious predictive models from many candidate variables.
assumptions: Appropriate model family; variable scaling and validated penalty choice.
example: Select biomarkers for predicting disease.

description: Combines L1 and L2 coefficient penalties for shrinkage and variable selection.
when_to_use: Build predictive models with many correlated candidate predictors.
assumptions: Appropriate model family; feature scaling; validated penalty choices.
example: Predict disease from correlated genetic measures.

description: Finds a regularized decision boundary or regression function, optionally via kernels.
when_to_use: Classify or predict outcomes with potentially nonlinear feature relationships.
assumptions: Suitable feature scaling, kernel, hyperparameters, and held-out validation.
example: Classify tumors from measured biomarkers.

description: Predicts using outcomes of observations nearest to a case in feature space.
when_to_use: Classify or predict when distance between observations is informative.
assumptions: Appropriate distance metric, feature scaling, tuning, and representative training data.
example: Classify risk based on similar patient profiles.

description: Uses Bayes' rule with conditionally independent feature likelihoods for classification.
when_to_use: Create fast probabilistic classifiers with many predictors.
assumptions: Approximate feature independence given class; suitable likelihood or smoothing assumptions.
example: Classify patient feedback as positive or negative.

description: Learns multilayer nonlinear relationships between inputs and outcomes.
when_to_use: Predict complex relationships with sufficient training data.
assumptions: Representative training data; architecture and regularization tuned without leakage.
example: Predict clinical outcomes from large patient feature sets.

description: Partitions data into a chosen number of clusters minimizing within-cluster squared distances.
when_to_use: Explore compact groups in multivariate numeric data.
assumptions: Meaningful Euclidean distances; chosen cluster count; sensitivity to scale and outliers.
example: Cluster participants by diet and physical activity measures.

description: Builds nested groupings of observations from a specified dissimilarity and linkage.
when_to_use: Explore possible cluster structure without initially fixing a final cluster count.
assumptions: Appropriate dissimilarity, linkage, scaling, and sensitivity to outliers.
example: Group regions with similar environmental exposures.

description: Finds dense groups of points and labels low-density points as noise.
when_to_use: Explore irregularly shaped clusters or spatial hotspots.
assumptions: Meaningful distance and neighborhood density settings; adequate data density.
example: Identify geographic concentrations of disease reports.

description: Detects unusual observations using short paths in randomized partitioning trees.
when_to_use: Flag anomalies without labeled abnormal cases.
assumptions: Representative background data and a meaningful anomaly threshold.
example: Detect unusual environmental sensor readings.

description: Models potentially nonlinear exposure-response effects distributed across current and past exposure lags.
when_to_use: Estimate delayed and cumulative effects of time-varying exposures.
assumptions: Adequate exposure history; defensible lag and basis specification; control of seasonality, trends, and confounding.
example: Estimate temperature-related mortality risk across subsequent days.
